decisions.reason: Waters et al. (2020) frame the efficacy of EIBI for children starting intervention after age 4 as the second primary aim of their study, reviewing Eikeseth, Smith, Jahr, and Eldevik (2002, 2007) in the Introduction (pp. 5-6) and enrolling children aged 18 to 75 months at treatment onset who exceeded Cohen et al.'s (2006) 42-month cutoff. Beyond testing baseline age in linear mixed models (Table 3) and comparing <42 versus >=42 months (Results, p. 18), the authors report an explicit empirical subgroup comparison for children past their fourth birthday at baseline (ages 4-6 years at EIBI onset: Year 3 gains of 9.10 to 22.46 points in EIBI versus -6.91 to 9.63 in SAU, with Year 3 scores 7.42 to 21.05 points higher in EIBI than SAU) and directly link these results to Eikeseth et al. (2007) in the Discussion (pp. 18, 20). Eikeseth et al. (2007; Behavior Modification, 31, 264-278; Crossref bibr14 DOI 10.1177/0145445506291396, unprinted in the article's reference list) is absent from shipped_rows.

literature on EIBI outcome in two ways: First, it examines whether outcomes
in a university-led multisite project (Cohen et al., 2006) could be replicated
with children seen by the same community agency outside of the project.
Second, it presents the first case-control study in the United States that
includes children with ASD who began intervention at varying ages throughout early childhood, ranging from 18 to 75 months. All children who did not
meet the age cutoff of 42 months for eligibility in a prior study (Cohen et al.,
2006) and/or who entered treatment after the end of the enrollment period for
that study were included in the current report.

Design and Procedures

Evaluations were conducted at baseline and annually for 3 years later for 94

This exact original study is already represented by shipped row 1849 (COHEN; AMERINE-DICKENS; SMITH, 2006, DOI 10.1097/00004703-200604002-00013, where the shipped title is truncated before the subtitle), so candidate target 0 is not a missing row.

decisions.reason: In the newly provided 24-page complete primary article (Waters et al., 2020), the authors test whether EIBI outcomes from a prior university-led multisite project (Cohen et al., 2006) could be replicated in a new, non-overlapping sample of 94 children with ASD (48 EIBI, 46 SAU, ages 18 to 75 months at onset) evaluated at baseline and annually for 3 years. Because the study collects and analyzes new empirical data to test the same hypothesis as Cohen et al. (2006), both the shipped row and blind target 0 accurately classify the record type as a replication.

(Cohen et al., 2006) and in other reports on EIBI (Eldevik et al., 2009).
Because these children were seen independently of the university-led project
that was involved in our previous study, the results indicate that favorable
outcomes can be sustained in a community setting. In addition, given the
wide age range of our sample, the results also support previous findings that
some children who are 4 to 6 years old at onset of EIBI can make substantial
gains in IQ, adaptive behavior, and school placement (Eikeseth et al., 2007).
The design of the present study did not allow for testing which factors made
it possible to maintain the effectiveness of EIBI outside of a university-led
project, but the setting did include features considered to promote sustainability
decisions.reason: In Results (pp. 14-19) and Discussion (pp. 18-20), EIBI significantly outperformed SAU across all longitudinal linear mixed-model time-by-treatment interactions (IQ, NVIQ, VABS Composite, Communication, Daily Living, and Socialization), Year 3 WIAT achievement subtests, less restrictive school placements, and typical-range functioning on most measures. Under Codebook Step 3 Rule 1, the authors state an explicit original-specific overall replication verdict for Cohen et al. (2006), concluding that gains were comparable to their prior study and that favorable outcomes were sustained independently in the community setting.
